**1. Animation.** In Characters & moves pick an ACT similar to what you want, edit frames/boxes and use *Copy to ACT slot…* to put a copy into an unused ACT number. New frames can use new images: import them with the Frame builder.

**2. Routine.** Characters & moves → *Move routines*. Clone the routine of a similar move. The cloner follows branches and the “continue next frame” pointers (`move.l #addr,(a4)`) and turns them into labels, so you can change ACT numbers (`($D2,a4)`…), damage (`($EF,a4)`), speed (`($50,a4)`), sounds and assemble it anywhere in free P1 space. Or start from the template.

**3. Input.** Either repoint an existing assignment (*Repoint … to the new routine*) so an existing motion triggers your move, or edit a motion definition in Command inputs, or trigger it from your own code (next section).

**4. Test.** With the emulator connected use ⚡ Assemble live + trigger P1. Or build the zip and run it in MAME with the debugger (`mame kof97 -debug`), break on your routine address (e.g. `bp 2FCF0` for Kyo's Oniyaki) and watch P1's ACT at $108172.

**Animations:** adjust each ACT's frame timing and boxes for the new art; add new ACTs into free slots with “Copy to ACT slot”.

**Armor:** KOF97 has no armor bit in the ACT. The game skips the hit reaction when the *attacker's* object byte +$E6 has bit 0 set. A small main-loop hook that sets the opponent's +$E6 bit 0 while your move's ACT is playing gives that move armor: you take the damage but keep moving (checked in FBNeo).

**C ROMs** — sprite graphics, in pairs (c1+c2, c3+c4…). Each 16×16 tile is 128 bytes: 64 in the odd file (bit planes 0–1) and 64 in the even file (planes 2–3). Tile number N lives at offset N×64 in both files of its pair.
**Characters & moves → Move list → Kyo**: each row is a complete move. Example: ↓→↓↘→ + A/C → routine `$315F8` (Mu Shiki) → ACTs D0, DB, D2, D7, DC…
**Counter hits:** hurt types $00, $0C, $10, $14, $18, $1C-$24 are counter-hit hurt boxes.
**Frame 529:** down-forward + C completes → ↓ ↘ + C; the command handler stores `$2FCF0` in `+$198` and the dispatcher runs (it is reached on 3 consecutive frames until the routine takes over).
**Frame 532:** `+0` = `$2FDE4` (phase 1), `+$1C6` = `$FDB4` (the crouch state it came from), ACT `$81`.
**Frame 604:** `jmp $1EAD8` puts `+0` back to `$F464`: Kyo can act again.
**Frames 521-524:** forward is held, the neutral state switches `+0` to walk (`$FBC6`) and the ACT to 1.
**Frames 525-528:** down is held, `+0` becomes the crouch states (`$FD02`, `$FDB4`), ACT `$15`.

**Frames 537-550:** the uppercut connects. Both fighters' `+0` are replaced by the hit freeze states (`$1633E`, `$163F4`, `$16402`); Iori goes on to `$18A3A` (hit reaction, ACT `$102`) and loses `$10` HP. Kyo's phase state comes back after the freeze.
**Frames 552-603:** phase 2 (`$2FE56`, ACT `$83`), the fall (`$2FE78`, `$2FEAA`) and the landing (`$2FECC`, ACT `$85`).

**Graphics:** export the old character's frames as PNG (Frame builder), redraw them, import them back into the same tiles or into free tile space. Keep the same frame sizes to reuse the existing image definitions.

**How a cancel really happens (traced in the code):** when an attack connects, the hit-freeze code ($163EE) calls `$1E5AA` every frame of the freeze. It reads the cancel nibble of the frame that hit; if it is non-zero it runs the character's command handler, and if you entered a special during the freeze whose type matches (4 = specials+supers, 8 = specials only, C = anything) it buffers that move and starts it when the freeze ends. So: the attack must touch the opponent, and the motion must be finished during the freeze.

**Installing it:** unzip into the FBNeo folder (the one with `support`) with “Extract here”, so the `.dat` and `.ips` files land directly in `support/ips/{name}/`. If they end up in a subfolder, FBNeo can't find them and IPS Manager stays grayed out. Keep the **original** `{name}.zip` in your roms folder. In FBNeo open Game → Load Game, select the game, press **IPS Manager**, tick the patch and press Play. The project notes are used as the patch description.

**Invincible frames:** a frame whose select byte has no hurt-box slots (e.g. `01` = only the attack slot, or `00`) has nothing to hit — fully invincible. Checked: 88 Shiki with only slot 0 selected passes through Iori's far C.

**Moves the game just executed** lists every routine that went through the dispatcher, with the frame and the player: do a move in the game and read its routine address here.
**Moves:** rewrite command definitions and clone/modify move routines as in “New move”.
**Neutral entry:** the `+0` value while standing still (`$F464` in KOF97); the entry a few bytes before it sets ACT 0 (`$F43E`).

**Neutral** (`+0` = `$F464`, entered through `$F43E`) is the state you are in when you can act. Every frame it calls the character's command handler through `+$194` (a per-character block, `+8` = handler), then normals and throws, then the joystick: holding forward switches `+0` to the walk state `$FBC6`, down to the crouch state `$FD02`, and so on.

**P ROMs** — 68000 program. P1 is mapped at $000000–$0FFFFF. Bigger games (KOF97: 4MB P2) page extra 1MB banks into $200000–$2FFFFF by writing to $2FFFF0. KOF tags each bank with its number in the first word (0001, 0002…).
**P1/P2 moves** lists the decoded move list of the character on screen; ⚡ starts any of them on that player.
**Palettes** are not in their own ROM: the game copies 16-color palettes from P ROM into palette RAM. Each sprite chooses one of 256 palettes; color 0 is transparent.
**Palettes:** write your 4 color variants over the slot's palette set.
**RAM** watches, writes and freezes any address. Everything is temporary: reset the game and it is gone.
**Routine of a move:** Characters & moves → Move list (decoded from the command handler), or do the move and read *Moves the game just executed* in the Live tab.

A Neo Geo sprite is a 16 px wide column of tiles; wide characters chain several columns. Tiles are read consecutively from the base tile. Alt+click a tile to open it in the tile browser.

A box is a rectangle around (x, y) from the character's feet, ±w wide and ±h tall. Sprites are stored facing **left**; when the character faces right the game mirrors both the sprite and box x. The reach of an attack box is `|x| + w` pixels in front of the character.

A fighter is a block of RAM (P1 `$108100`, P2 `$108300`). Writing a field changes the game only if the game reads that field after you write it and does not overwrite it first. That is why some edits need a **freeze** (written again every frame) and others work with a single write at the right moment.

A frame can carry up to four boxes (slots 0-3). Its **select** byte says which slots are live on that frame (bit 0 = slot 0 … bit 3 = slot 3). The game copies the live boxes into the player object (+$90, +$95, +$9A, +$9F, 5 bytes each) and the box id there is the type ÷ 4. The colors are the ones Fightcade's training mode uses:

A frame is several tiles: Neo Geo sprites are 16 px wide columns, tiles go downwards and characters chain columns. Use [Frame builder](tab:sprites) with the first tile number, columns and rows to see the whole frame.

Every object (each fighter, projectile, spark) is a RAM block whose first long, `+0`, is a code address: its **state**. Each frame the main loop walks the object list and calls that address. How a move is chosen: the command parser marks which motions of the character's check table were entered; the command handler (`${h}`) tests those bits and the buttons, then stores a **move routine** in the player object (+$198). The routine is the complete move: it sets damage, speed and sounds and plays its ACTs one after another (supers have many). Handler table: ${t} + char × 2.

How to cancel in game: the kick must **touch** the opponent, and the special's motion must be finished **during the hit freeze** — the game checks the cancel byte every frame of the freeze (code at `$163EE` → `$1E5AA`).

A recognised motion sets a bit; the character's command handler then stores a move routine at object+$198 and jumps to it.

The dispatcher does three things: it saves `+0` into `+$1C6`, reads `+$198` and jumps there. Writing the routine address into `+0` makes the object loop call it on the next frame, which is the same as being dispatched; writing it into `+$198` too keeps everything that reads the current move consistent. The routine then sets ACTs, damage, speed and sound itself, so the move is complete: hitboxes, projectiles, power cost and all.

`-debug` opens the MAME debugger. Useful commands: `bp 12914` (break on command check), `wp 108172,2,w` (watch P1 ACT changes), `dump`.
`P1` and `P2` are the object addresses. The facing is worked out from both fighters' x positions, so `6` always means forward. The program is verified in FBNeo on KOF97 (Kyo vs Iori):

`tools/live/injector.lua` runs Lua programs inside FBNeo, one step per frame. A program can press inputs (the game reads them like a real joystick), write memory and wait for things to happen. Use it from the **Lua injector** panel in the Live tab, from `tools/live/inject_demo.lua` without the app (put your code in `my_program.lua` next to it), or with `dofile("injector.lua")` in your own script.
